title: Is ChatGPT Massively Used by Students Nowadays? A Survey on the Use of Large Language Models such as ChatGPT in Educational Settings
extended_summary:
This paper examines how widely students are using large language models (LLMs) such as ChatGPT in educational settings, and whether usage differs by age, gender, and subject area. The authors are particularly concerned with how these tools may be reshaping learning practices, potentially supporting learning and productivity while also raising risks related to critical thinking, foundational knowledge, and emerging inequities such as an AI literacy gender gap.

The study uses a survey-based observational design. A Google Form questionnaire was administered in educational institutions, asking students about whether they used ChatGPT or equivalent tools in academic contexts, how often they used them, for which humanities and science topics, how satisfied they were with the outputs, whether they reworked the generated answers, what devices they used, and why some students did not use the tools. The analysis relies on descriptive statistics, chi-squared tests, residual analysis, and confidence intervals to identify associations across demographic groups.

The population consisted of 395 students aged 13 to 25 in France and Italy, spanning secondary school, high school, undergraduate, and graduate levels. The survey was conducted between May and October 2024 and was typically administered during class time under professor supervision. The authors note that the university sample was skewed toward science-related fields, and that some younger respondents required parental authorization. The study context was educational use of LLMs across both school and university settings rather than evaluation of a formal instructional intervention.

The main conclusions are that ChatGPT/LLM use is already very widespread, including among younger students, and increases with age. Male students reported higher use than female students, especially for science-related tasks, which the authors interpret as a potential emerging AI-related gender gap. Most users reported reworking model outputs, but systematic proofreading was less common among younger students. Students were generally satisfied with LLM outputs across age and gender groups. The authors argue that educational institutions should no longer ignore these tools and should adapt curricula and homework practices to integrate AI literacy, ethical use, critical evaluation, and awareness of limitations and environmental costs.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: A generative AI chatbot based on large language models used for conversational question answering, writing assistance, summarization, translation, and related language tasks.
identified_tools.use_case: Studied via a cross-sectional survey of students aged 13-25 in France and Italy about whether, how often, and for what academic purposes they used ChatGPT (or equivalent LLM tools), including humanities/science use, satisfaction, proofreading habits, and device preferences.

findings.finding_summary: In a survey of 395 students, 344/395 (87.1%) reported having used ChatGPT in an academic context. Usage was widespread across age groups, with nearly 70% of 13-16-year-olds reporting use and 89.7%-95.4% use in older groups; male students reported higher use than female students (93.8% vs 79.3%, χ2=16.84, p<10^-4).

Among ChatGPT users, systematic reworking/proofreading of outputs was limited, especially among younger students. Only 20% of students aged 13-16 reported always revising answers, and even among the oldest students systematic proofreading remained below 50%; the age-pattern difference was statistically significant (χ2=21.22, p=0.0017).

Students reported generally high satisfaction with ChatGPT outputs across age groups, with 'It was quite good' exceeding 50% in all age groups and no significant age difference in satisfaction (χ2=4.12, p=0.90). Satisfaction was also similar by gender (χ2=0.91, p=0.82).

The survey found notable gender disparities in ChatGPT use frequency and topical use. Male students were more likely to use ChatGPT frequently, particularly for science topics, while female students were less likely to report frequent use; science-topic use differed strongly by gender (χ2=41.18, p=5.98×10^-9), and humanities-topic use also differed (p=0.0011), which the authors interpret as a potential emerging AI literacy/technology gender gap.
findings.measure: Self-reported use frequency by gender and topic domain

quality_tier_rationale: This is an empirical primary study, but it is a cross-sectional survey rather than an RCT or quasi-experiment. Findings are based on self-reported usage and perceptions, with statistical tests for group differences but no causal design.
impact_tier_rationale: The paper shows substantial uptake and important behavioral disparities, but it does not estimate causal learning effects or standardized effect sizes on student achievement. Impact on outcomes is therefore meaningful but unclear in magnitude.
